scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: Nevermind de Nirvana (noviembre de 1991) llega al número uno el 11 de enero de 1992 y acaba con el reinado del lite metal. Los medios abrazan a Kurt Cobain y Eddie Vedder, las radios crean formatos «alternativos», la gran emisora de metal de Los Ángeles, KNAC, se vende en 1995 y MTV cancela Headbangers Ball en 1996; hasta Kerrang! se abre a la nueva moda, y los críticos, que crecieron con el rock universitario, ven por fin validado su gusto. El grunge no es metal aunque comparte la guitarra y la voz fuerte: alterna partes duras y suaves, canta el dolor y la desesperación, viste de tienda de segunda mano e identifica a la generación X con los débiles, frente al poder y el placer del metal («Somos pesados, pero no heavy metal», dice Krist Novoselic). Hacia 1998 el alternativo está moribundo.

podcast.title: First Meeting with Courtney Love (1989)
podcast.body: Kurt Cobain first encountered Courtney Love on January 21, 1989, when Nirvana was performing at the Satiricon Club in Portland, Oregon. Their initial interaction involved Kurt "unceremoniously help[ing] himself to Courtney's picture of beer." Afterwards, Kurt reportedly told friends that Courtney "looked like Nancy Spungin," referring to Sid Vicious's former girlfriend. "Courtney Love first saw Kurt Cobain when Nirvana played a show at the Satiricon Club in Portland, Oregon. The day was January 21st, 1989."

podcast.title: Developing Relationship with Courtney Love (1991)
podcast.body: After their initial meeting and an exchange of gifts (a heart-shaped box from Courtney), Kurt and Courtney reconnected on May 29, 1991, at a Butthole Surfers show in Los Angeles, one month after Nirvana secured their major record deal. Their "instant attraction" quickly escalated into a physical altercation involving Courtney punching Kurt, followed by wrestling and kicking, and then sharing drugs like Vicodin and high-powered cough syrup, leading to them becoming "pretty much inseparable." "There was instant attraction, especially after Courtney decided to punch Kurt in the stock. That led to some wrestling and kicking, and afterwards they shared some drugs, vikin' in and high powered cough syrup."

podcast.title: Alleged Nirvana Breakup Threat (September 10, 1993)
podcast.body: Tom Grant's theory posited that Kurt Cobain was prepared to dissolve Nirvana and join Hole with Courtney Love, suggesting this might have provided a motive for murder. In a September 10, 1993, interview with a French TV journalist, Kurt himself expressed a desire to quit Nirvana and join Hole, citing a higher level of musical connection with Courtney, but acknowledged it was "completely unrealistic" due to public perception intertwining them. "It's a nice thought, collaborations with Courtney. I'd like to, but to tell you the truth, I would rather just quit my ban and join whole."

podcast.title: Domestic Disputes and Police Involvement (1993-1994)
podcast.body: Kurt Cobain's turbulent relationship with Courtney Love led to several police interventions. On June 4, 1993, police were called to their Lake Washington Boulevard home to de-escalate a domestic situation, though charges were later dropped. On March 18, 1994, officers were again summoned after Kurt locked himself in a room with guns and threatened suicide, resulting in the confiscation of four firearms and 25 boxes of ammunition. "There was a police call to his home on Lake Washington Boulevard on June 4th, 1993."

podcast.title: Elden Hoke's Allegations of Murder-for-Hire (December 1993)
podcast.body: Elden Hoke (Eldu-Cher), frontman of the punk band The Mentors, publicly claimed in a 1996 High Times interview and a 1998 documentary that Courtney Love offered him $50,000 in December 1993 to kill Kurt Cobain. Hoke stated she said, "I need you to blow my old man's head off." He recounted an exchange outside a Los Angeles record store, corroborated by the owner, and said Courtney later called for him in March 1994. Although Hoke passed a lie detector test, his claims remain unverified and are often dismissed due to his unreliable narrator status. "Eldu-Cher claimed that in December 1993, Courtney offered him $50,000 to kill her husband."

podcast.title: Frequent Heroin Overdoses (1993-1994)
podcast.body: Kurt Cobain experienced numerous heroin overdoses, with nearly a dozen occurring in the ten months before his death. Notable incidents include an overdose on May 3, 1993, after injecting between $30 and $40 of cheap heroin, and another on May 9, 1993, from which paramedics rescued him with Narcan. A further overdose occurred in a New York hotel bathroom on July 23, 1993. "In the last 10 months of his life, Kurt Cobain OD'd almost a dozen times."

podcast.title: Hotel Room Destruction (December 1993)
podcast.body: In December 1993, Kurt Cobain and Nirvana destroyed a hotel room in St. Paul, Minnesota, while "really, really drunk." The damage amounted to $19,000 at the time, equivalent to about $37,000 today. "In December 1993, Nirvana destroyed a hotel room in St. Paul, Minnesota."

podcast.title: Isolation and "Rapunzel" Nickname (1993-1994)
podcast.body: Due to his increasing isolation and drug use, Kurt Cobain's friends began to refer to him as "Rapunzel," reflecting his tendency to rarely leave his room. This period of withdrawal contributed to concerns about his worsening depression and overall well-being. "He was so isolated that his friends began calling him Rapunzel because he rarely came down from his room."

podcast.title: Obsession with His Will and Financial Conflicts (1993-1994)
podcast.body: In the period leading up to his death, Kurt Cobain became increasingly preoccupied with writing his will, a concern noted by a nanny working in his house. This obsession coincided with significant financial disputes within Nirvana, as Kurt demanded a larger share of royalties and declined a $9 million Lollapalooza headline slot, further straining his relationship with bandmates and management. "And why had Kurt become so obsessed with writing his will?"

podcast.title: Ongoing Stomach Pain Issues (1993-1994)
podcast.body: For six months leading up to his death, Kurt Cobain suffered from severe stomach pain, for which he consulted nine different specialists on both coasts. Crohn's disease and IBS were ruled out, with possibilities including a severe form of acid reflux or a pinched nerve, which could explain why opioids temporarily relieved his pain. His personal journals extensively documented these struggles, including a desire to have a disease named after him and to create a rock opera about his gastric issues. "Let me just have my own very unexplainable rare stomach disease named after me."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Opioid Prescriptions and Self-Medication (1993-1994)
podcast.body: In an attempt to manage his chronic stomach pain, Kurt Cobain was prescribed various opioids, including Percodan, morphine, and bupranex, which provided temporary relief. However, he also engaged in self-medication with heroin, a habit that led to multiple overdose incidents in the final months of his life. "Perkadan and morphine were prescribed. If you go back through the scrolls and Kurt's now famous personal journals, you'll find many entries about a stomach."

podcast.title: Suicidal Ideation and Depression (1993-1994)
podcast.body: Following an overdose in July 1993, Kurt Cobain confessed in an interview with the British magazine The Face that he had "always been suicidal." His depression deepened in the fall of 1993, when he was frequently described as "strung out" and "semi-conscious." On legal documents related to a new book about Nirvana, he even listed his address as "hell on earth," underscoring his profound mental distress. "In the days after, he gave an interview to the British magazine The Face, where he convinced I've always been suicidal."

podcast.title: "Mystery Days" Leading to Death (April 3-5, 1994)
podcast.body: The three days between April 3 and April 5, 1994, leading up to Kurt Cobain's death, are largely considered a mystery, despite ongoing search efforts by a private detective and a missing person's report. During this time, Kurt was reportedly seen by various individuals around Seattle, including a taxi driver and friends, at a house he owned in Carnation, Washington, at a drug dealer's residence, and at several hotels. He also allegedly purchased a box of 20 gauge shotgun shells from a store called Seattle Guns. "The next couple of days, April 3, 4th, and 5th, 1994, are something of a mystery."

podcast.title: Ashes and Stolen Teddy Bear (Post-1994)
podcast.body: Following his cremation, some of Kurt Cobain's ashes were scattered along the banks of the Wishkah River in his hometown of Aberdeen, Washington. Courtney Love retained a portion of the ashes for a shrine in her home and kept more inside a teddy bear, which she carried with her. However, this teddy bear was stolen in 2008 and has never been recovered. "More were kept inside a teddy bear that she took with her, but that bear was stolen in 2008 and never recovered."

podcast.title: Attempted Suicide in Rome (March 3, 1994)
podcast.body: Kurt Cobain was found unconscious on the floor of room 541 at the Excelsior Hotel in Rome on March 3, 1994, after consuming up to 50 Rohypnol pills in addition to alcohol. He had been suffering from extreme depression, calling Courtney Love numerous times expressing hatred for "everything and everybody" after a series of European tour shows were canceled due to a throat issue. Courtney Love flew to Rome to meet him; they ordered room service and champagne before going to bed. He was transported to Umberto Polyclinic Hospital for his stomach to be pumped, and later to Rome American Hospital where he regained consciousness. He left a suicide note that, according to Courtney, read in part, "My doctor says I would have to choose between life and death. I'm choosing death." This incident was widely seen as an attempted suicide, predating his actual death by just over a month. "Nirvana and Kurt Cobain, who very nearly died in room 541 of the Excelsior Hotel in Rome on March 3, 1994."

podcast.title: Canceled Credit Card and Suspicious Activity (April 1-8, 1994)
podcast.body: On April 1, 1994, the day Kurt Cobain escaped rehab, Courtney Love allegedly canceled his Mastercard. Private detective Tom Grant stated that Courtney initially claimed "someone" was using the card, later clarifying it was Kurt and she wanted to track him. After Kurt's body was discovered, the Mastercard was reportedly missing. On April 4, there were multiple attempts to get cash advances ($5,000, $2,500, $1,500) over the phone, and on the morning of April 8, someone attempted to purchase $43.29 worth of flowers using the card. "On April 4th, the day before he died, someone tried to use the card."

podcast.title: Courtney Love's Missing Person Report Allegation (April 4, 1994)
podcast.body: Tom Grant claims that on April 4, 1994, Courtney Love filed a missing person's report for Kurt, impersonating his mother, Wendy Cobain. The report stated, "Mr. Cobain ran away from California facility and flew back to Seattle. He also body shotgun and maybe suicidal," a wording that Grant believes was intentionally crafted to frame Kurt's subsequent death as a suicide, guiding the police investigation towards that conclusion. "It was Courtney that called that report in. I believe one of the reasons she did that in my own personal opinion is so that she could word the report because the wording on that missing persons report turned out to be a pretty important thing in this investigation."

podcast.title: Crime Scene Anomaly Allegations (April 8, 1994)
podcast.body: Various claims were made about inconsistencies at the crime scene. Witnesses, including electrician Gary Smith, reported Kurt Cobain's hair looked "combed." Contrary to initial reports, he had not barricaded the room; a stool against the door was too short to prevent it from opening. Additionally, the forensics report stated "no legible prints" were found on the shotgun. These details, particularly the lack of clear fingerprints and the un-barricaded door, were cited by conspiracy theorists as evidence suggesting foul play. "Several witnesses, including Gary Smith, the nutrition, thought that Kurt's hair looked like it had been combed."

podcast.title: Death by Suicide (April 5, 1994)
podcast.body: Kurt Cobain died in the early morning of Tuesday, April 5, 1994, by suicide via shotgun, preceded by a massive heroin overdose. His body was found approximately two weeks later, on April 8. His family and friends were aware he was in trouble, especially after a previous suicide attempt at a hotel in Rome. On March 25, 1994, an intervention was held at his Seattle home with his wife Courtney Love, bandmates Chris Novoselic and Dave Grohl, touring guitarist Pat Smear, and members of Nirvana's management and legal team, lasting five hours. He seemed convinced to seek help and flew to LA on March 30 to check into the Exodus Recovery Center. However, he left on April 1 (Good Friday) by scaling a six-foot wall, flew back to Seattle, and disappeared. His final note, addressed to his imaginary friend "Boddah," was found in his pocket after he injected a large amount of Mexican black tar heroin and then used a Remington shotgun to kill himself in the greenhouse at his home. "He had injected so much heroin that he probably never even heard the gun go off."

podcast.title: Final Activities and Suicide Note (Early April 5, 1994)
podcast.body: In the early morning hours of Tuesday, April 5, Kurt Cobain woke up in his bed after sleeping in his clothes. He turned on MTV, found nothing interesting, then turned down the sound and put R.E.M.'s "Automatic for the People" album on his CD player. He lit three cigarettes while writing a note on a legal-sized notepad, addressed to his imaginary childhood friend, "Boddah." After finishing, he placed the note in his left coat pocket, retrieved a Remington shotgun, a box of shells, and a cigar box full of heroin from a hiding place. He also grabbed two towels from the linen closet, assuming someone might need them, and a can of Barks Root Beer from the fridge. He then went to a second-floor room in the greenhouse in his backyard, where he smoked five more cigarettes, added a few more lines to his note, and jammed the pen through the note into a pot of soil. He loaded three shells into the shotgun, cooked up $100 worth of Mexican black tar heroin into a syringe, injected it into his right arm, and before the full impact of the drug hit, he aimed and pulled the trigger. "The note was addressed to the imaginary friend he had known since he was a small child. It began to bata."

"Kurt hadn't been chilled that weekend, he would have gone to the bank and taken all the money out of the funds."

xref.title: Dave Grohl Joined Nirvana Because His Band's Bassist Broke Up with His Girlfriend (1990)
xref.body: Dave dropped out of high school to tour with DC punk band Scream for about three years. In the summer of 1990, bassist Skeater Thompson flaked out mid-tour in Los Angeles over the loss of his girlfriend, canceling multiple shows. Dave was left penniless (temporarily crashing with three female mud wrestlers) and doing cash tiling work for food money. He called Melvins leader King Buzzo (Kurt Cobain's idol), whom he'd met in Europe, who told him Kurt had a band needing a drummer. Dave flew to Seattle on September 21, 1990; four days later he auditioned and passed. Dave later wrote a song about Skeater Thompson called "Just Another Story About Skeater Thompson," available only on a cassette-only release made under the name "Late" in late 1990, titled *Pocket Watch*. "Dave has never forgotten Skeater Thompson and how thankful he is that Skeater had such bad girlfriend trouble."

xref.title: Joining Nirvana (1990)
xref.body: A few months after recording his Harling Talks AD demos, Dave Grohl received a call to audition for Nirvana. Buzz Osborne of The Melvins, who was idolized by Kurt Cobain, recommended Dave for the open drummer position. Dave flew to Seattle, arriving on Friday, September 21, 1990, and after an informal audition, became a member of the band without any explicit invitation, simply because "they just didn't ask him to leave." xref.title: Kurt Cobain Possibly Contributed Guitar and Vocals to Hole's "Asking For It" (1993, Rio)
xref.body: An unofficial version of Hole's "Asking For It" exists featuring a male voice on background vocals widely attributed to Kurt Cobain. It is believed to have been recorded at Ariola Studios in Rio de Janeiro in January 1993 when Nirvana was there for four days and Courtney Love was traveling with the band. The version did not appear on *Live Through This*. An official outtake from the same Rio sessions, a demo of "Miss World," appears on *My Body the Hand Grenade*. "It's not that big a leap to assume that the version of asking for it was also recorded during the Rio sessions."

xref.title: Rio de Janeiro Studio Sessions with Hole (1993)

xref.title: Encouragement from Seven Year Bitch Postcard (1994)
xref.body: The deciding factor in Dave Grohl's decision to continue making music after Kurt Cobain's suicide was a postcard he received from the Seattle band Seven Year Bitch. The band had endured significant tragedy themselves, losing a member to an overdose in 1992 and another to kidnapping, rape, and murder in 1993, yet they continued to make music. Their postcard read, "We know what you're going through. The desire to play music is gone for now, but it will return. Don't worry." This message convinced Dave that he was "put on this planet to make music" and that stopping would be wrong. "This convinced Dave that he needed to keep going."

xref.title: Final Show March 1, 1994; Death April 8, 1994 – The Vacuum That Reshaped 1994's Rock Landscape
xref.body: Nirvana played their final concert in Munich on March 1, 1994 — Kurt's voice was shot, the band was exhausted, and the rest of the European tour was canceled. On March 3, he deliberately overdosed on tranquilizers in a Rome hotel room. On March 18, police were called to his Seattle house after he locked himself in a room with guns. He agreed to enter rehab after an intervention, then escaped. His body was found April 8. The news was read on air: "Nirvana lead singer Kurt Cobain shot himself to death at a Seattle home yesterday." The effect on music fans was profound and prolonged. The loss of Nirvana's central narrative created a temporary opening that Green Day, The Offspring, Blur, and Oasis each rushed to fill. "Kurt's death was extremely traumatic. And the mourning continued for months."

xref.body: On May 29, 1996, a man calling himself "Reverend Jim Dillon" announced the founding of the Church of Kurt Cobain in Portland, Oregon, using Nirvana song lyrics as liturgy. The story received front-page coverage in *The Oregonian*, was picked up by MTV, and led the ABC Evening News with Peter Jennings. In reality it was a hoax — a local radio station had run a contest to see if listeners could trick *The Oregonian* into printing a fake story, and the winner was a man named Jerry Catel, who became "the Reverend Jim Dillon." His secondary intent was to make a statement about media shallowness and celebrity idolatry. "It was a hoax. The truth is that all this originated with a local radio station which staged a contest to see if listeners could get the Oregonian to print a fake story."

xref.title: Kurt Cobain's Death Controversy
xref.body: The short answer to whether Kurt Cobain was murdered is "no." However, many conspiracy theories persist, citing "unanswered questions" such as how he could inject a massive heroin overdose, put his gear away, and shoot himself before being incapacitated, the alleged change in handwriting on his suicide note, who used his credit card post-mortem, and why a room above the garden house wasn't checked during searches. These questions have fueled documentaries, books, and websites. Applying Occam's Razor, the "simplest answer is usually the correct one." Kurt was described as a depressed, unhealthy, hardcore heroin addict who associated with "very weird and bad people," had an obsession with guns, and was "certifiably suicidal." His body was so accustomed to heroin that a fatal dose might have had a delayed effect, allowing him time to put away a syringe and aim the gun. The murder theory is deemed "just chasing shadows," though the possibility of being wrong is acknowledged. "My short answer to this is no. Now there are all sorts of unanswered questions. How did Kurt manage to inject himself with a massive overdose of heroin, put his gear away in the maneuver the shot got in time before the drugs knocked him out? What about the fact that the handwriting on the suicide note appears to change? Who was using Kurt's credit card in the hours and days after he died? Why didn't anyone think to check the room above the garden house when they were searching for him?"

xref.title: Kurt Cobain's Vaguely Canadian Ancestry
xref.body: Kurt was born on February 20, 1967, at Aberdeen Community Hospital in Aberdeen, Washington. His paternal ancestry traces to a family from Skytown, County Tyrone, Ireland (spelled "Cobane"), who emigrated around 1875 to Cornwall, Ontario, where patriarch Samuel Cobain worked as a shoemaker. Census records confirm a Samuel Cobain, wife, and seven children in Cornwall. They subsequently moved to Gray's Harbor County, Washington, where Aberdeen is located. Kurt's great-uncle Delbert, on his mother's side, was a respected Irish tenor who appears in the 1930 film *King of Jazz* featuring Paul Whiteman and the young Bing Crosby. xref.title: Management of Kurt Cobain's Last House
xref.body: Following Kurt Cobain's death in 1994, his wife, Courtney Love, had the greenhouse where his body was found torn down in 1996. A year later, in 1997, she sold the 171 Lake Washington Boulevard East property to a Japanese businessman. When selling the house, Love included a unique clause in the contract, granting her the right to return at any time to remove a willow tree on the property, under which some of Kurt Cobain's ashes were located, and replant it elsewhere. "Courtney had the greenhouse where Kurt's body was found in 1994, torn down in 1996."

xref.title: Mastering of "Nevermind"
xref.body: Nirvana's "Nevermind" album, produced by Butch Vig, initially had a raw punk rock sound that the band found difficult to mix. Kurt Cobain chose Andy Wallace, known for his work with Slayer, to master the record, who added a sparkly edge to guitars, brought vocals forward, and made drums bigger. A final mastering pass was done by Howie Weinberg in Hollywood. The band famously disliked the final master as "too slick" but approved its release. "Kurt Cobain picked a guy named Andy Wallace, who at the time was well known for the sound he was able to get from Slayer."

xref.title: Medical Fetish – Anatomy Art, Gynecological Instruments, Full-Sized Medical Dummy on Tour
xref.body: Kurt Cobain's artistic aesthetic included a deep preoccupation with medical imagery and human anatomy that dated back to his grade school drawings. The artwork for *In Utero* features disassembled dolls, fetuses, and embryo-like forms. He reportedly collected vintage medical equipment and surgical instruments, including old gynecological devices well beyond basic medical tools. One account claims he kept a full-sized medical dummy at home and took it on tour in its own trunk. His journals (published by Courtney Love in 2002) reveal an obsession with bodily functions, vomit, urine, mucus, and excrement — consistent with his naming of his first band Fecal Matter. "Kurt had a full-sized medical dummy. Not only did he keep it around the house, but he toured with it."

xref.title: Outsider Music Figure and Mainstream Recognition (Early 1990s)
xref.body: Throughout the 1980s, Daniel Johnston released records that cemented his status as a low-fi hero and an important figure in "outsider music," a genre characterized by technically imperfect but passionately delivered performances. His unique approach and growing underground reputation eventually led to an MTV report on local music scenes. His fame significantly expanded in the early 1990s when Kurt Cobain was seen publicly wearing a Daniel Johnston T-shirt, elevating him to a major cult figure. "And in the early 1990s, when Kurt Cobain was spotted wearing a Daniel Johnston T-shirt, he became a major cult figure."

xref.title: Perceived Feud with Nirvana

However, Kurt later clarified that the perceived feud was largely his fault and that he should have targeted the record company for pushing Pearl Jam onto the "grunge bandwagon" without their full realization or will. Eddie Vedder now agrees with Kurt's assessment of what was happening to Pearl Jam at the time. "That never was a feud. I slagged them off because I didn't like their band. It was my fault. I should have been slagging off the record company instead of them."

xref.title: Plagiarism Claim Against Nirvana
xref.body: Killing Joke's song "80s" (1985), co-written by Jazz Coleman, was observed to have a guitar riff strikingly similar to Nirvana's "Come As You Are" (1991). The situation regarding a lawsuit remains unclear, with conflicting reports on whether action was taken or dropped after Kurt Cobain's death, or simply considered but not pursued for financial/personal reasons. xref.title: Post-Nirvana Feud with Courtney Love
xref.body: A significant feud developed between Dave Grohl and Courtney Love after Kurt Cobain's death. The first public evidence of bad blood was a 1999 interview where Dave Grohl, when asked for his favorite Hole song, replied "Teenage Horror" because it was "the one I know Courtney actually wrote," implying she didn't write others. Courtney Love subsequently attacked Dave in the media over legal disputes concerning Nirvana's music, accusing him of being sexually obsessed with Kurt Cobain and claiming he hired Taylor Hawkins as Foo Fighters' drummer because of Hawkins' resemblance to Kurt. "The first evidence I can find of some kind of bad blood was an interview Dave gave in 1999, a few years after the food fighters got going."

xref.title: Postcard to Dave Grohl
xref.body: Seven Year Bitch sent a postcard to Dave Grohl following Kurt Cobain's suicide, understanding the grief he was experiencing.
